hook.line: English says have done for things that just happened: I've eaten, she's arrived. In Bogotá people use the plain past for all of that. Get this right and you sound like you learned your Spanish here.
hook.en:
Have you eaten yet?
Yes, I've already eaten.

examples.en: I went to the bank today.
Have you eaten yet? (to a friend)
I made the coffee this morning.
Have you been to Leticia? (to a friend)

rule:
English uses have done for lots of things that are over: I've eaten, she's arrived, I've been to the bank today. Colombian Spanish doesn't. If it happened and it's finished, even five minutes ago, use the plain past:
*Hoy fui al banco.* I went to the bank today.
*¿Ya comiste?* Have you eaten yet?
*Vale ya llegó.* Vale has already arrived.

Save *he*, *has*, *ha* for two jobs:
your life so far, with no time attached: *¿Has ido a Leticia?* *Nunca he estado allá.*
things that haven't happened yet: *Todavía no he terminado.* (The plain past works here too: *Todavía no terminé.*)

A quick test: can you point to when it happened (today, this morning, at six, yesterday)? Then it's the plain past.
smallPrint: Teachers call this the split between the preterite (*pretérito indefinido*) and the present perfect (*pretérito perfecto*). Spain uses the perfect for today's events; most of Latin America doesn't.

options: Did you go to Leticia today?
Have you ever been to Leticia?

readAndPick.es: He estado en Cartagena dos veces.
options: I went to Cartagena on two days.
I'm in Cartagena for two days.
I speak to Mariana every day.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick and type the whole sentence: *Hoy ___ al banco.* (*fui* or *he ido*) I went to the bank today.
yourTurn.why: It's over and it happened today, so the plain past: *fui*.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick and type the whole sentence: *¿___ a Leticia?* (*Fuiste* or *Has ido*) Asking a friend if she's ever been.
yourTurn.why: Ever, in your life, with no time attached: *has ido*.

yourTurn.prompt: Ask a friend: Have you eaten yet?
yourTurn.why: In Colombia, have you eaten yet is the plain past with *ya*.

yourTurn.prompt: Tell Vale: I've already made the coffee.
yourTurn.why: It's done, so the plain past, even though English says I've.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: I've never been to Leticia.
accept: No he estado nunca en Leticia.
yourTurn.why: Never, across your whole life: *nunca he*.
Arriving is over and done, so the plain past: *llegó*.

yourTurn.prompt: Turn it into your whole life: *No comí ajiaco.* (I've never eaten ajiaco.)
yourTurn.why: Never, with no day attached, takes *nunca he* and *comido*.

pitfalls.why: Fine in Madrid, but in Colombia something finished takes the plain past, even today.
People will understand you, but here they ask it with the plain past.
A time that's over, like *ayer* or *anoche*, never takes *he*, anywhere.

personal: Write two true lines: something you did today (plain past) and a place you've never been (*nunca he*).
